When you "brood," you sit with something heavy in your mind and just... stay there. You think about something sad, painful, or troubling — again and again — in a dark, silent, withdrawn way. You don't move on from it. You don't solve it. You just dwell on it, turning it over in your head, unable to let it go.

Think of it as the opposite of "shaking something off." Brooding is when a thought wraps around you and you let it sit there, weighing on you.

1. The Figurative Meaning — What People Do (Most Common)

This is how you'll encounter "brood" most of the time.

When a person broods, they:

  • Think about something for a long time, not just briefly
  • Think about it in a dark, heavy, unhappy way
  • Are usually quiet and withdrawn while doing so
  • Are often alone
  • Find no solution — they're not problem-solving, just dwelling

After losing the match, she sat alone by the window, brooding.

He brooded over the argument for days, replaying every word in his head.

Don't just brood about your failures — do something about them.

The subject of brooding is almost always something painful: a mistake, a loss, an insult, a failure, a regret, a grievance. You don't brood about happy things.

2. The Literal Meaning — What Birds Do

Originally and literally, "brood" describes what a bird does when it sits on its eggs to keep them warm until they hatch. The bird covers the eggs with its body, staying very still, in silence, for a long stretch of time.

The hen brooded her eggs for three weeks.

You may not use this meaning often in daily life, but it's important because it's the foundation of the word. And you can see the beautiful connection: a bird brooding over eggs — still, silent, huddled in one place, not moving on — is exactly the image carried into the human meaning. A person brooding is emotionally doing the same thing: sitting still, in silence, hovering over one thought.

3. The Atmospheric Meaning — What Dark Things Do

"Brood" can also describe something dark and heavy hanging over a place in a threatening, oppressive way. This is mostly used in literary or descriptive writing.

Storm clouds brooded over the valley.

A heavy silence brooded over the empty town.

Here, the sky or silence acts like a brooding person — looming, dark, still, and heavy. It gives a place a feeling of unease or gloom.

Understanding what makes "brood" distinct from similar words will sharpen your sense of it.

  • Think — Neutral. Could be about anything, positive or negative.
  • Worry — More anxious and active. Worry feels restless; brooding feels still.
  • Sulk — More about refusing to communicate after feeling wronged. Sulking is pouting. Brooding is deeper, darker, more internal.
  • Ruminate — Very close to brood. But ruminate is more neutral and intellectual (it can even be positive reflection). Brood always carries darkness and emotional pain.
  • Dwell on — Perhaps the closest phrase. But brood is more intense and more emotional.

The defining qualities of brood that separate it from all of these: darkness + silence + stillness + prolonged duration + no resolution.

Brood is almost always followed by over, on, or about:

  • brood over something — the most common
  • brood on something — slightly more formal
  • brood about something — also natural

You can also use it without any preposition when the context is clear:

He just sat there, brooding.

You'll frequently encounter brooding as an adjective, and it's worth knowing:

  • A brooding person — someone who seems deep in dark, heavy thoughts; quiet, intense, and inward.
  • A brooding look / silence / atmosphere — heavy, dark, and full of unspoken emotion or threat.
  • A brooding sky / landscape — dark and threatening, with a sense of something looming.

He was a tall, brooding man who rarely smiled.

The painting captured the brooding atmosphere of the moors.
To brood is to think about something painful or troubling in a prolonged, silent, and deeply dark way — sitting with it emotionally rather than moving past it.
